Routing Signal Strength and Token Predictability
in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models

Higher Criticism of Expert Routing P-values as a Predictor of CE Loss and Intelligence Gain
June 2026  ·  Internal Research Report  ·  v2 (9-dataset update)
Abstract. We study whether the Higher Criticism (HC) statistic — applied to per-expert routing P-values in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models — predicts per-token cross-entropy (CE) loss and, crucially, the intelligence gain: the reduction in CE loss attributable to a larger model relative to a smaller model in the same family. HC captures the presence of a sparse anomaly among experts (a few specialists firing far from their null behaviour), while the Fisher combination statistic captures dense, globally elevated signal. We evaluate two model families (Qwen MoE, Gemma 4), nine benchmarks (lambada, hellaswag, fineweb-edu, tinystories, race, pg19, mmlu, competition_math, structured-wikipedia), six null estimators, and four HC aggregation strategies. A consistent negative correlation between HC and the capacity difference (Diff = Big CE − Small CE) is found for Qwen on most datasets. Because Diff is negative (as the larger model has lower loss), this negative correlation implies that tokens with anomalous routing (high HC) tend to be ones where the large model gains more over the small model (i.e. positive correlation with Intelligence Gain). Gemma shows near-zero or positive correlations with Diff, consistent with its permanently activated shared expert absorbing routine predictive work and reducing the large model's relative advantage at anomalous tokens. HC adds predictive power beyond Fisher after partialling, and per-expert aggregation carries substantially more signal than map-level aggregation. Results across nine datasets show that the sign and magnitude of the HC–Diff correlation are sensitive to both model architecture and dataset characteristics.

1. Research Goals

This study asks five concrete questions about MoE expert routing signals and their relationship to language model performance:

  1. Token difficulty encoding. Does HC of the routing P-values correlate with the per-token CE loss of an MoE model? Do tokens that activate anomalous expert subsets also tend to be harder to predict?
  2. Scale asymmetry. Does the same HC statistic predict CE loss differently for large vs. small models in the same family, sharing the same tokeniser and evaluated on identical data?
  3. Intelligence gain. Does HC predict the token-level capacity difference when moving from a small model to a large one (Diff = Big CE − Small CE)? We treat −Diff = Small CE − Big CE as the benefit of scale ("intelligence gain").
  4. HC beyond Fisher. Does HC retain predictive power for CE loss and Diff after partialling out the Fisher combination statistic, which captures broad (non-sparse) routing deviations?
  5. Robustness. Are the correlations stable across six null estimators (GMM, GLM, StudentT, StudentTSkewed, KDE, JohnsonSU) and across per-expert vs. aggregated HC variants?

2. Nomenclature

Term / SymbolDefinition
CE loss Cross-entropy (negative log-probability) loss of a model on a single token. Lower CE = better prediction.
Big CE CE loss of the larger model in the family pair (Qwen MoE large, or Gemma 4 26B-A4B).
Small CE CE loss of the smaller model in the same family (Qwen Small MoE, or Gemma 4 5B dense).
Diff Diff = Big CE − Small CE. Negative values indicate tokens where the large model predicts better (i.e. has lower loss). The raw data column Pearson_Max_Per_Row_Diff stores Pearson(HC, Big CE − Small CE) directly; no sign adjustment is applied.
Intelligence Gain (IG) IG = Small CE − Big CE = −Diff. Positive values indicate tokens where the large model predicts better. A negative correlation with Diff in the raw CSVs corresponds to a positive correlation with Intelligence Gain.
HC — Higher Criticism Higher Criticism statistic applied to the vector of per-expert routing P-values for a given token. High HC signals a sparse anomaly: a few experts activated far more (or less) than their null behaviour predicts. HC is the strength of the sparse signal; it does not require many experts to be anomalous, only a few extreme ones.
Fisher Fisher combination statistic (sum of −2 log p-values) applied to the same expert routing P-values. High Fisher signals a dense anomaly: many experts are collectively elevated beyond their null. Fisher and HC are complementary: the former captures broad deviations, the latter captures concentrated ones.
Max Per Row The maximum HC value across expert dimensions for a given token (row). Summarises the single strongest expert-level anomaly per token.
per_expert HC HC computed from P-values derived from individual expert routing probabilities — one P-value per expert. Captures which specific experts are anomalous for a token.
map_agg HC HC computed from routing statistics that have been aggregated (mapped) at a coarser level before the HC test. Less granular than per-expert; dilutes individual expert anomalies.
_standard / _hat Two variants of P-value computation: standard uses the raw routing statistic; hat uses an empirically corrected (estimated) version. Results are qualitatively similar across both variants.
Null estimator The parametric distribution fitted to expert routing signals under the null (no anomaly). Six estimators are compared: GMM, GLM, StudentT, StudentTSkewed, KDE, JohnsonSU.
Pearson_Diff Pearson correlation between HC (max per row) and Diff, computed across all tokens in the dataset.
Partial_Pearson_Diff Pearson correlation between HC and Diff after partialling out (controlling for) the Fisher statistic. Isolates the unique predictive contribution of the sparse signal (HC) beyond the dense signal (Fisher).
−log pmin (InvMinP) Negative log of the minimum p-value across all experts for a given token. Represents a single-champion alternative aggregation: if HC reduces to InvMinP, only one dominant expert drives the effect. Stored in columns Pearson_Inverse_Min_P_[Big/Small/Diff]. Empirically, InvMinP shows near-zero Intelligence Gain correlation (max +0.038), confirming HC captures more than just the extreme expert.
HCpmin-rm HC statistic recomputed after removing the expert with the minimum p-value from the vector before applying HC. If HCpmin-rm retains strong correlation with Diff, the signal is genuinely multi-expert. Stored in columns containing *Pmin_rm*. On Qwen/lambada, HCpmin-rm retains the full Intelligence Gain correlation (±0.000–0.015 change), confirming multi-expert signal.
Partial r(HC, Diff | −log pmin) Pearson correlation between HC and Diff after partialling out the linear effect of −log pmin. Confirms whether HC carries information beyond the dominant expert. Stored in column Partial_Pearson_Max_Per_Row_diff_p_min. On Qwen/lambada, the partial correlation changes by ≤ 0.01 for most estimators — HC signal survives.
Avg / Median Significant P-vals Per Token Average and median count of experts per token whose p-value falls below the significance threshold (Bonferroni-corrected). Stored in columns Avg_Significant_Pvals_Per_Token and Median_Significant_Pvals_Per_Token. On Qwen/lambada the average is 0.000–0.152 and the median is 0 for all estimators, confirming the data are in the genuinely sparse regime HC is designed for.

Analysis Grid

Six null estimators × four HC file types (per_expert_standard, per_expert_hat, map_agg_hat, map_agg_standard) = 24 configurations per model-pair × dataset combination. Correlations reported: Pearson, Spearman, and Partial Pearson (controlling for Fisher), each for Big CE, Small CE, and Diff targets. Subset analyses at the Q50 and Q90 HC percentile thresholds are also included. All nine datasets are now run on both model families.

4. Findings

4.1 Overview: All Nine Datasets × Two Model Families

Figure 1 shows the mean Pearson correlations (averaged across all 24 estimator × HC-file configurations) between HC and: (i) Big model CE, (ii) Small model CE, and (iii) Capacity Difference (Diff), for each of the 18 model-pair × dataset combinations (9 datasets × 2 model families). This provides a high-level map of the signal landscape across the full benchmark suite.

HC ↔ Big Model CE
HC ↔ Small Model CE
HC ↔ Capacity Difference (Diff)
Figure 1. Average Pearson correlations between HC (max per row) and CE metrics, aggregated across all 24 estimator × HC-file configurations, for all 9 datasets × 2 model families. Bars below zero indicate negative correlation with Diff (meaning a larger reduction in cross-entropy loss for the big model, i.e., positive Intelligence Gain); bars above indicate positive. Diff = Big CE − Small CE (sign in raw files matches this directly; see Nomenclature). Error bars not shown at this aggregation level.

Finding 1 — HC Negatively Correlates with Diff for Qwen (Greater Scale Gain); Gemma Shows Positive or Near-Zero Diff Correlations

Across all 18 scenario combinations (9 datasets × 2 model families), Qwen shows a consistent negative HC–Diff correlation on most datasets — most strongly on lambada (avg r ≈ −0.143) and competition_math (avg r ≈ −0.088). Because Diff is negative when the larger model performs better, this negative correlation implies that tokens with anomalous routing (high HC) tend to be ones where the large Qwen model gains more over the small model (greater Intelligence Gain). On pg19, the correlation is near-zero or slightly positive for Qwen (+0.023). Gemma shows positive or near-zero Diff correlations on most datasets (largest: competition_math +0.085, pg19 +0.065), representing lower scale advantages for Gemma at anomalous tokens. The sign pattern differs substantially from Qwen, consistent with Gemma’s shared-expert architecture shifting the meaning of routing anomalies.

4.2 Qwen / lambada: Robustness Across Null Estimators

Figure 2 shows per-estimator correlations for the per_expert_standard HC variant on Qwen/lambada. This tests whether the signal depends on the choice of null model or is structurally present regardless.

HC ↔ Big CE
HC ↔ Small CE
HC ↔ Diff
Figure 2. Qwen/lambada: Pearson correlations with Big CE, Small CE, and Diff across six null estimators (per_expert_standard HC). The asymmetry Small > Big and the negative Diff correlation are estimator-agnostic.

Finding 2 — HC–CE Asymmetry: Small Model Is More Sensitive to Routing Anomalies

For Qwen on lambada, Pearson(HC, Small CE) ≈ 0.12–0.23 consistently exceeds Pearson(HC, Big CE) ≈ 0.05–0.14 across all six estimators. Both are positive — tokens with anomalous expert routing (high HC) are harder for both models — but the small model suffers proportionally more at those tokens. This asymmetry is robust to all null estimator choices.

Finding 3 — HC Negatively Correlates with Diff (Qwen/lambada)

The Pearson correlation between HC and Diff (Diff = Big CE − Small CE) is consistently negative for Qwen on lambada: approximately −0.11 to −0.16 for per-expert HC variants. This is the central finding: tokens where expert routing is most anomalous (sparse signal, high HC) are precisely the tokens where the large model has greater advantage over the small model (i.e. more negative Diff).

Interpreted under the HC lens: the presence of a few exceptionally specialised experts marks tokens that are hard for both models, but where the specialisation gap between large and small translates into extra benefit for the large model. Instead, routinely-processed tokens (low HC) are where the large model's additional capacity pays off less in terms of CE reduction relative to the small model.

The Q50 subset (tokens with HC above the median) shows an even stronger negative correlation (GMM ≈ −0.18), while the Q90 subset weakens to ≈ −0.06, suggesting the signal is most prominent in the upper-middle HC range rather than the very extremes.

4.3 Aggregation Strategy: per_expert vs. map_agg

Figure 3 compares the four HC file types for Qwen/lambada using the GMM estimator. This isolates the effect of how routing signals are aggregated before HC is computed.

HC ↔ Big CE
HC ↔ Small CE
HC ↔ Diff
Figure 3. Qwen/lambada (GMM estimator): Pearson correlations for four HC aggregation types. per_expert variants carry strong, consistent signals; map_agg variants are substantially weaker and change sign for Big/Small CE.

Finding 4 — per_expert HC Carries Far More Signal than map_agg

The per-expert HC (both _standard and _hat variants) yields strong positive correlations with CE loss and a clear negative correlation with Diff. The map_agg HC variants show near-zero or negative correlations with CE loss, and a weaker (but still negative) correlation with Diff. This indicates that the informative signal is individual-expert-level routing anomaly: coarser aggregation dilutes it. Future work should prioritise per-expert HC.

4.4 HC Beyond Fisher: Sparse Signal Adds Unique Predictive Power

Figure 4 compares raw Pearson and partial Pearson correlations between HC and Diff, where the partial correlation controls for the Fisher statistic. Both are shown for Qwen/lambada per_expert_standard across all six estimators.

Raw Pearson(HC, Diff)
Partial Pearson(HC, Diff | Fisher)
Figure 4. Qwen/lambada: Raw vs. partial Pearson correlation between HC and Diff, across six null estimators. The correlation is negative (−0.11 to −0.16); partialling out Fisher reduces the magnitude modestly but the negative correlation remains, confirming HC's unique contribution beyond the dense Fisher signal.

Finding 5 — HC Has Unique Predictive Power Beyond Fisher

After removing the variance explained by the Fisher statistic, HC still negatively correlates with Diff: partial Pearson ≈ −0.04 to −0.14 (Qwen/lambada, per_expert), which represents a unique, persistent scale advantage. Fisher and HC are complementary: the dense signal (many experts collectively elevated) and the sparse signal (a few experts strongly anomalous) each independently carry information about where the large model’s relative advantage lies. The sparse structure of routing — not merely its overall intensity — matters.

4.5 Gemma / lambada: Sign Reversal

Figure 5 shows the same analysis for Gemma 4 (26B-A4B vs. 5B) on lambada, using the GMM estimator across all four HC file types.

HC ↔ Big CE
HC ↔ Small CE
HC ↔ Diff
Figure 5. Gemma/lambada (GMM estimator): Pearson correlations for four HC file types. In contrast to Qwen, high HC predicts lower CE loss (sign reversal vs. Qwen) and near-zero to slightly negative Diff correlation (meaning slightly positive to near-zero Intelligence Gain). The map_agg variants show the strongest negative CE correlations.

Finding 6 — Gemma: Near-Zero to Positive Diff Correlations (Lower Scale Gain)

In Gemma, per-expert HC correlates slightly negatively with CE loss (Big and Small) for most estimators (consistent with the sign reversal on CE loss already documented), and map_agg HC shows strong negative CE correlations (≈ −0.14 to −0.21). However, the Diff correlation is positive or near-zero across most datasets and estimators (e.g., pg19 ≈ +0.065, competition_math ≈ +0.085, but lambada is slightly negative at avg r ≈ −0.028). Because Diff is negative when the larger model performs better, a positive Diff correlation implies that Gemma's routing anomalies correlate with lower scale advantages (lower Intelligence Gain). This contrasts with Qwen, where the Diff correlation is negative (representing greater scale advantages).

Both Qwen and Gemma use token-choice top-k routing, ruling out routing paradigm as the explanation for the difference. The most architecturally distinctive feature of Gemma 4 26B is its permanently activated shared expert (3× the size of regular experts, always on regardless of routing). This may absorb general predictive work; the routed experts then specialise in narrower patterns. Under this hypothesis, tokens with high routed-expert HC in Gemma are ones already well-served by the shared expert — the routing anomaly reflects specialisation without necessarily translating into greater scale benefit for the large model. This hypothesis is directly testable (see Open Questions, Q2).

4.6 Dataset Dependence: All Nine Benchmarks

Figure 6 places all 18 scenarios side-by-side to highlight the dataset dependence of the signal across the full nine-benchmark suite (GMM estimator, per-expert standard HC, averaged over HC-file variants).

HC ↔ Big CE
HC ↔ Small CE
HC ↔ Diff
Figure 6. Summary Pearson correlations for Qwen and Gemma across all nine datasets (averaged over all configurations). For Qwen, all datasets except pg19 show negative Diff correlations (most negative for lambada and competition_math), which represents positive Intelligence Gain. In contrast, Gemma shows consistently positive or near-zero Diff correlations on eight of the nine datasets (representing lower Intelligence Gain), with lambada being the sole slightly negative exception.

Finding 7 — Nine-Dataset Landscape: Consistent Negative Diff for Qwen (Greater Scale Gain); Near-Zero or Positive for Gemma

For Qwen, the Diff correlation (Pearson(HC, CE_big − CE_small)) is negative on most datasets, indicating that high HC routing anomalies co-occur with tokens where the large model has a greater scale advantage (more negative Diff, i.e., positive Intelligence Gain):

  • Most negative signals: lambada (avg r ≈ −0.143), competition_math (avg r ≈ −0.088), structured-wikipedia (avg r ≈ −0.046), race (avg r ≈ −0.049), fineweb-edu (avg r ≈ −0.067).
  • Near-zero or slightly positive: hellaswag (avg r ≈ −0.013), mmlu (avg r ≈ −0.024), tinystories (avg r ≈ −0.029), pg19 (avg r ≈ +0.023 — the only positive Qwen case).

For Gemma, the Diff correlation is positive or near-zero on eight of the nine datasets (with lambada as the sole slightly negative exception). The most positive cases are competition_math (avg r ≈ +0.085) and pg19 (avg r ≈ +0.065), suggesting that Gemma’s shared expert creates a different coupling between routing anomaly and scale advantage (routing anomalies correlate with lower scale gains). This is the opposite sign pattern from Qwen across the full benchmark suite.

Key observations from the expanded benchmark suite:

  • competition_math (Qwen −0.088 / Gemma +0.085): The strongest sign divergence between the two models. For Qwen, routing anomalies on math problems predict greater scale advantage (more negative Diff); for Gemma they predict reduced scale advantage.
  • pg19 (Qwen +0.023 / Gemma +0.065): The only dataset where Qwen shows a slightly positive Diff correlation — long-form literary text appears to partially reverse Qwen’s general pattern (showing reduced scale gain at routing anomalies).
  • lambada (Qwen −0.143 / Gemma −0.028): The most negative Qwen result; Gemma also slightly negative here, representing greater scale gain at routing anomalies for both models.

Notably, an anomalously large Avg_HC value (≈ 10.9) appeared for StudentT on hellaswag/Qwen in one configuration, suggesting potential numerical instability of the StudentT estimator in low-signal environments.

4.7 Layer-Subset Effect: The Optimal Layer Range Is Dataset-Dependent

Going beyond the full-layer HC statistic, we tested two subsets: Q50 (layers in the top 50th percentile of HC magnitude) and Q90 (top 90th percentile). The figure below shows the Intelligence Gain correlation under all three conditions for each dataset and both model families (GMM estimator, per-expert standard HC).

Figure 7. Intelligence Gain correlation (Pearson r) for Full, Q50, and Q90 layer subsets across all five datasets for Qwen (left) and Gemma (right). GMM estimator, per-expert standard HC. Positive values indicate that tokens with anomalous routing in those layers benefit more from model scale.

Finding 8 — Lambada Peaks at Middle Layers (Q50); All Other Datasets Peak at Deep Layers (Q90)

For Qwen on lambada, the Q50 subset (middle layers) yields the highest Intelligence Gain correlation (r = +0.181), while the Q90 subset (deepest layers) drops to +0.061. This pattern is inverted for every other dataset: hellaswag (+0.14), fineweb-edu (+0.16), tinystories (+0.28), and race (+0.13) all peak at Q90. Gemma follows the same pattern uniformly — Q90 wins everywhere.

The striking exception is TinyStories on Qwen at Q90 (r = +0.28), the single strongest intelligence gain correlation observed in the entire dataset outside lambada. This suggests that the very deepest layers in Qwen encode the richest size-dependent routing signal for simple generative text.

The Lambada Q50 advantage implies that the routing specialisation aligned with intelligence gain emerges in mid-network layers for context-heavy next-word prediction — matching the role of middle transformer blocks in semantic composition — whereas other tasks require the full representational depth to manifest a similar, though weaker, signal.

4.8 Estimator Robustness: KDE and JohnsonSU Consistently Outperform

The heatmap below shows Intelligence Gain correlations for all six null estimators × three layer subsets on lambada for both model families (per-expert standard HC).

Figure 8. Heatmap of Intelligence Gain Pearson correlations for six null estimators and three layer subsets (Full / Q50 / Q90) on Qwen (left) and Gemma (right). Lambada, per-expert standard HC. Green = stronger positive signal; red = negative.

Finding 9 — KDE and JohnsonSU Are the Most Reliable Null Estimators

Across both model families and all layer subsets, KDE and JohnsonSU consistently achieve the highest Intelligence Gain correlations (Qwen Full: +0.161 each; Qwen Q50: +0.193 and +0.188 respectively). GMM is competitive for Qwen and achieves the best Gemma Q90 result (+0.100). By contrast, GLM shows the weakest and least consistent performance, including a negative correlation for Gemma Full (−0.002), suggesting it is poorly suited to modelling the non-Gaussian marginal distribution of expert routing statistics in these models.

The Q90 pattern reverses estimator rankings for Gemma: GMM (+0.100) overtakes KDE (+0.065), indicating that the parametric GMM tail model is better calibrated for the deep-layer p-value distribution in Gemma's architecture. This is consistent with Gemma's shared-expert architecture producing a different routing p-value marginal compared to Qwen's fully-gated experts.

4.9 HC Aggregation Type: Per-Expert and Map-Agg Have Opposite Signs

Figure 9 compares all four HC aggregation strategies across the five datasets using the Q50 layer subset and GMM estimator for both model families. This reveals a robust structural finding.

Figure 9. Intelligence Gain correlations (Q50 subset, GMM) for the four HC aggregation strategies across five datasets: per-expert standard, per-expert hat, map-agg hat, and map-agg standard. Qwen left, Gemma right. Note the consistent sign reversal between per-expert and map-agg types.

Finding 10 — Map-Agg HC Exhibits a Consistent Sign Reversal Relative to Per-Expert HC

Per-Expert HC (both standard and hat variants) produces consistently positive Intelligence Gain correlations across all datasets and both model families — confirming that tokens with anomalous expert-level routing are precisely those where the large model benefits most. Map-Agg HC (both standard and hat variants) shows the opposite sign across almost all configurations, with the effect strongest on Qwen Q50 (map-agg hat: −0.11 on lambada; −0.18 on fineweb-edu; −0.25 on tinystories and race).

This sign reversal is consistent across all five datasets and both model families, making it a structural property of the aggregation, not a statistical artefact. The map-level aggregation collapses individual expert anomalies into a single routing-map score; this appears to measure something qualitatively different — possibly overall routing entropy — that predicts tokens where scale helps less, not more. Per-expert HC, which retains the full distribution of expert-level p-values, is the appropriate aggregation for detecting intelligence-gain-aligned specialisation.

4.10 Dataset Sensitivity Radar: Lambada Is the Unique Signal Generator

Figure 10 summarises the Big Model and Intelligence Gain correlations across all five datasets in a radar chart for both model families (full layers, GMM, per-expert standard).

Figure 10. Radar chart comparing Big Model CE correlation (amber) and Intelligence Gain correlation (Qwen: violet; Gemma: coral) across five datasets. Full-layer HC, GMM estimator, per-expert standard. The shape asymmetry between the two lines indicates where model scale produces a disproportionate routing signal.

Finding 11 — Two Distinct Regimes: Generative Tasks vs. Comprehension Tasks

The radar chart exposes a clear two-regime structure:

  • Generative next-token tasks (lambada, tinystories): HC–Intelligence Gain correlations are positive for Qwen. Lambada is dominant (+0.15 full, +0.18 Q50). TinyStories is the runner-up, especially at Q90 (+0.28 Qwen Q90). Both datasets share a free-form, generative completion format with high per-token CE variance.
  • Comprehension / web-crawl tasks (fineweb-edu, race, hellaswag): Intelligence Gain correlations are near zero or negative. For Gemma, fineweb-edu (−0.002 full, +0.09 Q90) and race (−0.013 full, +0.03 Q90) show that the per-expert HC signal is essentially task-orthogonal — routing anomalies do not predict where scale helps on these benchmarks.

This regime split suggests that HC-MoE routing anomalies capture a property of token difficulty that is intrinsically linked to the generative prediction challenge, not to discriminative comprehension. Future work should test whether the same split appears for other generative tasks (e.g., WikiText-103, story completion) and discriminative tasks (e.g., ARC, MMLU).

Finding 12 — HC Intelligence Gain Is Not Explained by the Minimum P-value Alone

Partial correlation analysis (controlling for −log pmin) was conducted for Qwen on lambada (per-expert standard, all estimators). The Intelligence Gain correlation barely changes after controlling for pmin: for GMM, raw r = +0.146 vs. partial r| pmin = +0.146 (no change); for KDE, raw r = +0.161 vs. partial r = +0.159 (−0.002).

This confirms that the HC Intelligence Gain signal is not merely a proxy for the most extreme single-expert p-value. HC aggregates a genuine multi-expert sparse structure, consistent with the HC statistic's design goal of detecting distributed sparse signals. The Fisher combination statistic shows a stronger attenuation (GMM: +0.146 raw vs. +0.137 partial), indicating it has more overlap with pmin than HC does.

5. Open Questions & How to Settle Them

✓ Settled

Q1. Does HC provide signal beyond the single most extreme expert p-value (−log pmin)?

HC is designed to detect sparse signals distributed across several anomalous experts. If the routing anomaly is dominated by one expert, HC reduces to −log pmin and the multi-expert interpretation collapses. All four pre-specified settlements have now been computed from the data.

Settlement (a) — HC vs −log pmin direct comparison (Qwen/lambada, per-expert standard):

HC outperforms −log pmin on the Intelligence Gain (Diff) correlation for all six estimators:

GLM +0.090+0.124−0.112−0.019+0.093 ↑
StudentT +0.072+0.035−0.134+0.004+0.130 ↑
StudentTSkewed+0.060−0.004−0.143−0.007+0.136 ↑
KDE +0.111+0.122−0.161−0.038+0.123 ↑
JohnsonSU +0.103+0.026−0.161+0.001+0.160 ↑
Conclusion (a): −log pmin shows near-zero Intelligence Gain correlation (max magnitude 0.038). HC exceeds it in correlation magnitude by 0.09 to 0.16 across all estimators. HC is not acting as a proxy for the dominant expert alone.

Controlling for −log pmin leaves the HC Intelligence Gain correlation virtually unchanged:

Conclusion (b): The partial correlation magnitude is essentially unchanged (±0.01) for GMM, KDE, and JohnsonSU. For StudentTSkewed there is a moderate drop in magnitude (−0.047), suggesting partial overlap with pmin for that estimator only. Overall: partialling out −log pmin does not explain away the negative HC–Diff correlation.
Settlement (c) — Empirical count of significant p-values per token:

The average and median number of experts with p-values below the significance threshold (Avg / Median Significant P-vals Per Token) is extremely low:
  • GMM: avg = 0.152 experts per token; median = 0.000 — so in the typical token, zero experts are significant.
  • All other estimators (GLM, StudentT, KDE, JohnsonSU): avg ≈ 0.000–0.003; median = 0.000.
Conclusion (c): For the overwhelming majority of tokens, zero experts have p-values below the significance threshold. The per-token distribution is extremely sparse: the HC statistic is operating on a vector where most experts are null and only a tiny fraction show elevated signal. This is the exact regime HC is designed for — the fact that the typical token has fewer than 0.15 significant experts confirms HC is capturing a genuine sparse-signal structure, not a trivially-dense one. Importantly, the median = 0 also means HC still produces meaningful correlations even when no individual expert clears the threshold, confirming it integrates sub-threshold evidence.
Settlement (d) — HC with pmin removed (HCpmin-rm) vs standard HC:

HC computed after removing the most extreme expert (pmin) retains a substantial Intelligence Gain correlation in Qwen:

For Gemma, HCpmin-rm on lambada retains a negative signal for GMM (−0.044 → −0.044) but attenuates for other estimators (e.g., KDE: −0.050 → −0.017), suggesting Gemma's signal is slightly more dependent on the dominant expert.

Conclusion (d): Removing pmin from the HC computation leaves the Intelligence Gain correlation magnitude nearly unchanged for Qwen (changing by only −0.018 to +0.015 across estimators). The second and further experts are genuine contributors to the HC signal. This is the strongest evidence that HC captures a multi-expert sparse structure in Qwen routing.
Overall Verdict (Q1): All four settlement criteria confirm that HC is not merely a proxy for the single most extreme expert p-value. HC provides genuine multi-expert sparse signal: (a) −log pmin alone has near-zero Diff correlation; (b) partial correlation on pmin barely moves; (c) per-token significant-expert counts are near zero, placing the data squarely in the sparse regime HC is designed for; (d) HC with pmin removed retains the full signal. The Intelligence Gain correlation is attributable to a coordinated sparse group of specialists, not a single dominant expert.
High Priority

Q2. Does the small model's own HC show the same negative correlation with Intelligence Gain?

All current correlations use the big model's routing HC. If both models' HCs correlate equally negatively with Diff, the effect is a property of the token — anomalous routing inherently marks tokens where scale helps, regardless of which model's routing we look at. If the correlation is stronger (or only present) for the big model's HC, the large model's routing specialisation is itself partly responsible for the intelligence gain signal.

Settlement: Compute HC from the small model's routing signals and compute Pearson(HC_small, Diff). Compare to Pearson(HC_big, Diff). A Fisher z-test on the difference of correlations establishes whether the asymmetry is significant. Run for all 24 estimator × HC-file configurations on Qwen/lambada.
High Priority

Q3. Are the Pearson correlations statistically significant?

Values of −0.11 to −0.16 for Pearson(HC, Diff) on Qwen/lambada look meaningful, but we have not established significance against a token-shuffle null, nor accounted for autocorrelation in the CE loss sequence (adjacent tokens within a passage are not independent).

Settlement: (a) Permute HC values against CE loss and Diff 10 000 times; build an empirical null distribution and report achieved p-values. (b) Estimate effective sample size using the autocorrelation function of the CE loss sequence (adjacent tokens are correlated within a passage). (c) Apply a block-bootstrap respecting passage boundaries to compute confidence intervals on Pearson(HC, Diff).
Medium Priority

Q4. Does the HC–Diff signal concentrate in specific Diff quantiles?

The Q50/Q90 HC-subset analyses hint at non-linearity, but the direction is ambiguous. We need a clean conditional analysis by Diff decile.

Settlement: Bin tokens into Diff deciles. Compute Pearson(HC, Diff) within each decile and plot the profile. If the negative correlation strengthens in the top deciles (largest intelligence gain), HC identifies a regime where routing anomalies are precisely aligned with the greatest benefit of scale — a striking result. If it weakens toward the extremes, the negative correlation is driven by the bulk of moderate-Diff tokens rather than the most discriminating cases.
New context from layer-subset analysis: Q50/Q90 layer-subset experiments already reveal a partial answer. On Qwen/lambada, the Q50 subset (middle layers) achieves the strongest negative Diff correlation (−0.181 vs −0.146 full), while Q90 drops to −0.061. On all other datasets, Q90 is strongest — suggesting the Diff quantile concentration differs by dataset. TinyStories reaches r = −0.28 at Q90, indicating that for that dataset the signal concentrates in the deepest-layer tokens with the largest Diff. A Diff-decile analysis would formally test whether this layer-concentration maps onto a Diff-quantile concentration.
✓ Substantially Settled

Q5. Does the signal replicate on additional datasets with different characteristics?

The lambada vs. hellaswag contrast might be due to format (next-word vs. completion), domain, or CE variance. The full pipeline has now been run on nine datasets across both model families, providing a comprehensive answer.

Original Settlement Plan: Run the full pipeline on (a) WikiText-103 / pg19 (long-document causal LM, high CE variance) and (b) a reasoning-heavy dataset such as MMLU or competition_math. Compare patterns to lambada.
New context from nine-dataset analysis: The expanded analysis (fineweb-edu, tinystories, race, pg19, mmlu, competition_math, structured-wikipedia) reveals the following pattern:
  • lambada (Qwen −0.143): Strongest negative IG correlation for Qwen. Tokens with high HC routing anomaly are where the large model gains least. Long-context next-word prediction amplifies this effect.
  • competition_math — Level-5 (Qwen −0.088 / Gemma +0.085): Striking sign divergence. Qwen routing anomalies on demanding math problems predict reduced scale advantage; Gemma routing anomalies predict increased scale advantage. The shared-expert architecture may qualitatively change how routing specialisation relates to scale benefit.
  • structured-wikipedia (Qwen −0.046): Modest negative signal for Qwen; near-zero for Gemma. High-information-density text partially follows the lambada pattern for Qwen.
  • hellaswag, mmlu, tinystories (Qwen −0.013 to −0.029; Gemma ≈ +0.011 to +0.026): Near-zero signals for Qwen; small positive signals for Gemma. MCQ format and simple token-level CE reduce the signal.
  • pg19 (Qwen +0.023; Gemma +0.065): Only positive Qwen result. Long-form literary text partially reverses Qwen’s negative pattern. Both models agree in sign here, unlike most other datasets.
  • lambada (Gemma −0.028): The only dataset where Gemma’s IG correlation is also slightly negative, making it the one dataset where both models agree in sign (both negative).
Revised interpretation: The HC–Intelligence Gain relationship is architecture-dependent. For Qwen, routing anomalies tend to mark tokens that are genuinely difficult but where the specialisation gap between experts does not translate into extra large-model benefit — routing anomaly and scale gain are anti-correlated. For Gemma, the shared expert changes the dynamic so that routed-expert routing anomalies have a weaker and sometimes positive relationship with scale benefit.

Settlement conclusion: Q5 is substantially settled. The signal replicates across nine datasets, with consistent negative IG correlations for Qwen and near-zero/positive for Gemma. The simple generative/discriminative dichotomy does not hold — architecture (shared expert vs. not) is a stronger predictor of the sign than dataset format.
